questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: A transfer must debit one account and credit another, with neither change left alone after failure. Which ACID property is illustrated?
questions.explanation: Atomicity gives the transaction all-or-nothing effects. The debit and credit must belong to the same transaction for this guarantee to cover both.
questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: Which ACID property requires a correctly designed transaction to preserve the database's declared integrity rules?
questions.explanation: Consistency concerns transitions between valid database states. The application and declared constraints must correctly express the intended business rules.
questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: Which ACID property concerns interference between concurrently executing transactions?
questions.explanation: Isolation controls how transactions observe and interact with concurrent work. The guarantees depend on the selected isolation level.
questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: Which ACID property concerns retaining committed changes after a failure covered by the system's persistence guarantees?
questions.explanation: Durability concerns committed results. Logs, storage and configuration implement the promised guarantees; no system survives every possible destruction of all copies.
questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: A transaction reads a value written by another transaction that has not committed. What is this anomaly?
questions.explanation: A dirty read exposes uncommitted data that may later be rolled back.
questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: A transaction reads a row twice and sees a changed value after another transaction commits an update. What is this anomaly called?
questions.explanation: A non-repeatable read concerns changed data in a row already read. A dirty read instead involves uncommitted data.
questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: Repeating a predicate query returns additional matching rows after another transaction commits inserts. Which phenomenon is illustrated?
questions.explanation: A phantom changes the set of rows satisfying a predicate. It differs from changing a value in an already observed row.
questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What does serializable isolation aim to guarantee for successfully committed transactions?
options: Every transaction sees every later commit immediately
An outcome equivalent to some serial execution
Every transaction is guaranteed to commit without retry
No locks or validation are ever needed
All transactions must physically run one at a time
questions.explanation: Serializable execution can still run concurrently. A DBMS may abort a transaction to preserve serializability, requiring an application retry.
questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: Under ordinary shared/exclusive locking, which locks can coexist from different transactions on the same item?
options: Only one shared lock in every case
A shared lock and a conflicting exclusive lock
Any lock combination without compatibility checks
questions.explanation: Shared locks are compatible with other shared locks. An exclusive lock conflicts with another transaction's shared or exclusive lock on the same item.
questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: T1 waits for a lock held by T2, while T2 waits for a lock held by T1. What condition is present?
questions.explanation: The circular wait prevents either transaction from progressing without intervention, such as aborting one transaction or releasing resources.
questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: Which concurrency-control approach commonly performs work and then validates whether it can commit safely?
options: Permanent exclusive locking of the whole database
questions.explanation: Optimistic approaches check for conflicts during validation rather than requiring every conflict to be prevented by advance locking.
questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What is the essential two-phase locking rule?
options: Only two transactions may run at once
A lock can never be released
Every transaction must hold exactly two locks
After releasing a lock, a transaction acquires no new locks
questions.explanation: Two-phase locking has a growing acquisition phase and a shrinking release phase. Standard 2PL ensures conflict serializability but can still deadlock.
questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What is the central write-ahead logging rule for an update?
options: Delete the transaction log before commit
Treat the log as an optional index
Always flush data pages before writing their log records
Keep all log records only in volatile memory
Persist the required log information before flushing the corresponding changed data page
questions.explanation: WAL ensures that recovery information is stable before the corresponding data page can reach persistent storage. Commit also requires the appropriate commit-related log records to be persisted under the promised durability mode.
questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: In undo/redo recovery, what is UNDO used for?
options: Reversing changes of transactions that must not take effect
questions.explanation: UNDO reverses changes that must be rolled back, such as uncommitted updates that reached persistent pages under a steal policy.
questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: In undo/redo recovery, what is REDO used for?
options: Reapplying required logged changes not yet reflected in data pages
Removing every transaction's locks before it starts
Eliminating the need for a transaction log
Replacing all backups with an empty file
questions.explanation: REDO reapplies logged changes when necessary. Schemes such as ARIES may redo history before undoing loser transactions; recovery algorithms differ in detail.
questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What is a main purpose of a database checkpoint?
options: Convert every index into a primary key
Reduce the amount of recovery work or log scanning needed
Guarantee that no transaction can ever fail
questions.explanation: A checkpoint records a useful recovery position and state. Its exact contents and flushing behaviour depend on the recovery algorithm; it is not a substitute for backups.
questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: In buffer management, what does a steal policy permit?
options: Prohibiting all writes before every commit
Flushing a page containing an uncommitted transaction's changes
Discarding all dirty pages without logging
questions.explanation: Steal permits uncommitted changes to reach data pages, creating a need for appropriate UNDO information during recovery.
questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What does a no-force policy permit at commit?
options: The commit record must never be persisted
Some changed data pages may remain unflushed
All logs must be erased immediately
Every transaction must lose its changes
Every data page must already be on disk
questions.explanation: No-force avoids flushing every changed page at commit. Appropriate REDO logging supports later recovery of committed changes not yet in data pages.
questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: A simple undo/redo recovery model must retain T1's committed effects and discard T2's uncommitted effects after a crash. Which actions express that goal?
options: UNDO T1 and retain every T2 change
REDO T1 as needed and UNDO T2 as needed
Delete both transactions' log records first
Always preserve T2 because it ran later
questions.explanation: Committed effects must survive and uncommitted effects must not remain visible. Actual algorithms can perform additional steps, including repeating history before undo.
questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: A failed data disk loses database pages, while a usable backup and required archived logs survive. Which recovery approach is appropriate?
options: Treat a checkpoint record as a complete replacement for the lost pages
Delete all archived logs before restoration
Restore the backup and replay the required logs
questions.explanation: Media recovery requires recoverable data copies and the necessary logs. Crash recovery alone cannot reconstruct arbitrary lost pages without sufficient surviving information.
questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What does a conventional full backup contain?
options: All selected data within the backup's defined scope
Only changes since the latest incremental backup
Only the names of missing files
Only changes since the latest full backup
questions.explanation: A full backup captures the selected scope. It does not necessarily mean every disk or every service on the entire server.
questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: A differential backup contains changes since the latest full backup. Which set normally restores to that differential's point?
options: Only the latest differential without its base
The full backup and that latest differential
Every earlier differential but no full backup
questions.explanation: A differential is cumulative relative to its full base. Unlike a conventional incremental chain, earlier differentials are not normally required for this restore point.
questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: A full backup is taken Sunday, then conventional incremental backups Monday and Tuesday, each covering changes since the preceding backup. What restores Tuesday's point?
options: Sunday full, Monday incremental and Tuesday incremental
Sunday full alone with no later changes
Sunday full and Tuesday incremental only
questions.explanation: This incremental chain depends on both increments after its full base. Backup products can use different terminology, so the dependency rule is explicit.
questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: What is generally required for point-in-time database recovery to a chosen time after a base backup?
options: Only a B+ tree root key
The usable base backup and an unbroken sequence of required transaction logs
Only a checkpoint timestamp without data or logs
Only a list of active usernames
questions.explanation: Point-in-time recovery restores a suitable base and replays logs to a supported target. Missing required log segments can prevent reaching that target.

references.title: PostgreSQL: continuous archiving and point-in-time recovery

questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: Which statement correctly describes RAID 0?
options: Striping without redundancy; one member-disk failure can lose the array
Mirroring with guaranteed survival of any disk failure
A scheme storing two copies of every block
questions.explanation: RAID 0 distributes data across disks for capacity and performance but has no redundancy. RAID is not protection against every deletion, corruption or site failure.

references.title: Database System Concepts: physical storage and RAID
Linux kernel: multiple-device and RAID administration

questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: A conventional two-disk RAID 1 mirror uses two equal 2 TB disks. Ignoring metadata and spare space, what is usable capacity?
questions.explanation: Both disks store mirrored data, so usable capacity equals one member's capacity: 2 TB. Mirroring provides redundancy, not a backup history.

references.title: Database System Concepts: physical storage and RAID
Linux kernel: multiple-device and RAID administration

questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: Which conventional RAID level uses distributed single parity and tolerates one member-disk failure?
questions.explanation: RAID 5 uses distributed single parity and normally requires at least three disks. It cannot in general tolerate two simultaneous member failures.

references.title: Database System Concepts: physical storage and RAID
Linux kernel: multiple-device and RAID administration

questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: Which conventional RAID level uses dual distributed parity and can tolerate any two member-disk failures?
questions.explanation: RAID 6 provides two independent parity protections and normally requires at least four disks. It is still not a substitute for backups.

references.title: Database System Concepts: physical storage and RAID
Linux kernel: multiple-device and RAID administration

questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: A four-disk RAID 10 is striped across mirror pairs {A1,A2} and {B1,B2}. Which two-disk failure necessarily destroys one complete mirror pair?
questions.explanation: Losing both members of the same pair removes that pair's data. Losing one disk from each pair can be tolerated in this conventional layout.

references.title: Database System Concepts: physical storage and RAID
Linux kernel: multiple-device and RAID administration

questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: A RAID 5 array has four equal 2 TB disks. Ignoring metadata and spare capacity, what is usable capacity?
questions.explanation: Single-parity capacity is (N−1) × S: (4−1) × 2 = 6 TB. This assumes equal disks and no dedicated spare in the four members.

references.title: Database System Concepts: physical storage and RAID
Linux kernel: multiple-device and RAID administration

questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: A RAID 6 array has six equal 2 TB disks. Ignoring metadata and spare capacity, what is usable capacity?
questions.explanation: Dual-parity capacity is (N−2) × S: (6−2) × 2 = 8 TB. All six stated disks are active array members.

references.title: Database System Concepts: physical storage and RAID
Linux kernel: multiple-device and RAID administration

questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: dbms
questions.question: A conventional RAID 10 uses four equal 2 TB disks in two two-way mirror pairs, then stripes across the pairs. What is usable capacity, ignoring overhead?
questions.explanation: Two-way mirroring leaves half the raw capacity: 4 × 2 / 2 = 4 TB. The paired layout is stated because RAID implementations can support other layouts.

references.title: Database System Concepts: physical storage and RAID
Linux kernel: multiple-device and RAID administration

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What is a primary role of an operating system?
options: Translate every high-level program into machine code
Manage hardware resources and provide services to programs
Act only as a spreadsheet engine
questions.explanation: The OS manages resources such as CPU time, memory, files and devices, and exposes services that applications can use.

references.title: Arpaci-Dusseau and Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP: introduction to operating systems

questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: os
questions.question: Why do processors distinguish user mode from kernel mode?
options: To require a separate CPU for every user
To restrict privileged operations and protect the system
To give every application unrestricted hardware access
To make every application part of the kernel
To prevent all interrupts during application execution
questions.explanation: User mode restricts privileged operations. Controlled entry into kernel mode lets the OS perform protected operations on an application's behalf.

references.title: OSTEP: limited direct execution, protection, system calls and interrupts
University of Illinois Chicago: operating-system structures

questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: os
questions.question: An application requests an OS service such as opening a file. Which interface normally provides controlled entry into the kernel?
questions.explanation: A system call transfers control to an OS entry point with appropriate privilege checks. A library function may wrap a system call; the two are not identical concepts.

references.title: OSTEP: limited direct execution, protection, system calls and interrupts
OSTEP: files, directories, permissions and links

questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: os
questions.question: Which event is normally an asynchronous hardware interrupt?
options: A function returns to its caller
An instruction accesses an unmapped page
A device signals that an I/O operation has completed
A program deliberately invokes a system call
questions.explanation: A device interrupt arrives independently of the current instruction's intended operation. Divide errors and page faults are synchronous exceptions; a system call is an intentional controlled request.

references.title: OSTEP: limited direct execution, protection, system calls and interrupts
OSTEP: I/O devices, interrupts, DMA and buffering

questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: os
questions.question: Which description best matches a monolithic kernel architecture?
options: Every application contains its own physical processor
The OS cannot support loadable modules
All OS services must run as separate user processes
The kernel contains only a boot menu
Many OS services run within the kernel's privileged address space
questions.explanation: A monolithic design puts substantial OS functionality in kernel space. Monolithic kernels can still be modular; Linux is a familiar example.

references.title: University of Illinois Chicago: operating-system structures

questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What distinguishes a microkernel design?
options: Require all software to use real-mode addressing
Put every device driver and file service permanently in one large kernel
Run all applications without memory protection
Keep a small privileged core and move many services to user space
questions.explanation: Microkernels keep a limited set of essential mechanisms privileged, with many services in user-space servers communicating through messages. The exact split depends on the design.

references.title: University of Illinois Chicago: operating-system structures

questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: os
questions.question: In a layered OS design, how are components principally organized?
options: Into one interrupt handler per application variable
Into processes that all bypass the kernel
Into levels that use services of lower levels
Into a single application with no interfaces
Into files sorted only by filename
questions.explanation: Layering organizes OS functions into levels with defined interfaces. Lower layers provide services used by higher layers.

references.title: University of Illinois Chicago: operating-system structures

questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What is a principal goal of time-sharing on an interactive system?
options: Guarantee that each task finishes before a hard deadline
Prevent preemption in every scheduling policy
Run exactly one job until it completes
Keep every program permanently on the CPU
Share CPU time to provide responsive service to multiple tasks or users
questions.explanation: Time-sharing frequently switches CPU service among runnable tasks to support interactive responsiveness. It does not itself guarantee hard real-time deadlines.

references.title: Arpaci-Dusseau and Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP: introduction to operating systems
OSTEP: CPU scheduling, turnaround, response, SJF and Round Robin

questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: os
questions.question: Which requirement characterizes a hard real-time task?
options: It must be an interactive desktop application
Its specified deadline must be met
It may ignore all deadlines under light load
Its average response time alone is sufficient
It must use the highest CPU clock available
questions.explanation: Hard real-time correctness includes meeting the required deadline, as well as producing the right result. This differs from merely aiming for a good average response time.

references.title: Linux kernel: deadline scheduling and hard real-time tasks

questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What is the principal role of a hypervisor?
options: Manage user accounts within a single guest OS only
Manage virtual machines and their access to underlying resources
Schedule threads solely within one application process
Translate one process virtual address through a page table
Provide only a guest file-system namespace
questions.explanation: A hypervisor presents and manages virtual-machine resources so guest systems can run with controlled sharing and isolation. It is also called a virtual machine monitor.
questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: os
questions.question: How does a process differ from a program stored on disk?
options: A process cannot have an address space
A program must always contain several processes
A process is necessarily a device driver
A process is an executing instance with runtime state and resources
A process is only the source-code filename
questions.explanation: A program is passive code/data; a process is a running instance with an address space, execution state and managed resources. Multiple processes can execute the same program.
questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: os
questions.question: In the basic five-state process model, what does Ready mean?
options: Waiting for an I/O event before it can run
Not yet created by the OS
Able to run but waiting to be assigned a CPU
questions.explanation: A ready process can execute once scheduled. A blocked/waiting process first needs an event such as I/O completion.
questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: os
questions.question: A running process requests blocking disk I/O that cannot complete immediately. What is its normal next state?
options: Ready while the I/O remains incomplete
Running indefinitely on the same CPU
questions.explanation: Blocking I/O makes the process wait for an event. The scheduler can use the CPU for another ready process.
questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: os
questions.question: In the basic process-state model, where does a blocked process normally move when its awaited I/O completes?
options: Always directly to Running without scheduling
questions.explanation: I/O completion makes the process runnable. It normally enters the ready queue before a scheduler dispatches it.
questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: os
questions.question: A timer interrupt causes a running process to lose the CPU while remaining runnable. Which transition occurs?
options: Running to Waiting for disk I/O
questions.explanation: Preemption removes the CPU from a runnable process, so it returns to Ready. Blocking is a different transition caused by waiting for an event.

references.title: OSTEP: CPU scheduling, turnaround, response, SJF and Round Robin

questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: os
questions.question: In a state model that includes suspension, what does Ready Suspended mean?
options: Terminated but waiting for its parent to collect status
Waiting for an I/O event while already executing
Currently using the CPU in kernel mode
Runnable apart from needing to be brought back into main memory
questions.explanation: Ready Suspended distinguishes a swapped-out runnable process from a blocked one. It must be resumed into memory before it can be dispatched. This state belongs to an extended model, not the basic five-state model.

references.title: University of Illinois Chicago: processes, scheduling and IPC

questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application

questions.subject: os
questions.question: In the basic process-state model, which event causes a running process to enter Terminated?
options: The process exits or is ended
It is selected from the ready queue
questions.explanation: Exit ends the process's execution. Quantum expiry causes preemption; blocking input causes waiting. Systems may retain exit-status information temporarily after execution ends.
questions.studyReason: Curated degree-level foundation or representative exam-style application
